svg.title: The four-step security method from assets to technology, and the asset classification ladder that sets the budget
svg.desc: Four steps in order. Assets: what are we protecting, and how bad is it if each one is exposed, altered or unavailable - the artifact is a classified asset list, and the failure is that every asset gets classified as important. Threats: who would want it and how would they get it - the artifact is a STRIDE table with the attack surface, the failure is a generic threat list copied from the internet. Controls: which control, placed where, at what cost - the artifact is a control matrix mapping each threat to prevention or detection with an owner, the failure is buying a product and then inventing a threat for it. Verify: how do we know it works - the artifact is a test case per control, the failure is trusting the vendor datasheet. Bottom: the classification ladder, four tiers. Tier one, regulated or life-safety, gets the strongest control and the only 24x7 monitoring. Tier two, business-critical, gets segmentation plus logging. Tier three, internal, gets baseline hygiene. Tier four, public or guest, gets isolation only and nothing more, because spending on guests is spending taken away from tier one. A footer says the ladder is the yardstick for every later argument about budget.
svg.text: Four steps, in this order, each with one artifact and one characteristic failure
Skip a step and the argument moves to technology, where it can never be settled, because the disagreement was about assets.

THE ASSET LADDER - the yardstick every later budget argument is measured against
Every budget argument is really a tier argument. Say "this is tier 2" and the discussion becomes finite; say "this is important" and it never ends.
Practical note: the ladder is only useful if the tier is written on the asset record, not in someone's head. The tier is what the firewall policy, the backup policy and the patching window all quote.
And tier 4 is not a punishment: it is the only way to stop guest access from consuming the security budget of tier 1.
